Newly hatched larvae of the axillary seabream measure approximately 0.25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.25 centimeters] in total length at birth, a modest size typical of marine sparids that produce numerous small offspring. At this stage, the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.0000832 grams [Wwb = 0.0000832 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves allocated to each individual. These values were obtained from laboratory-reared specimens maintained at a stable temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], conditions under which the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching from the chorion, was recorded as 2.0 days [ab = 2.0 days] after fertilisation. This rapid eclosion is characteristic of pelagic egg layers that rely on exogenous food sources soon after hatching. The yolk-sac larva stage is therefore brief, with the onset of exogenous feeding occurring shortly thereafter. Comparative data from related Pagellus species suggest that the small neonatal size and low hatchling mass are linked to an energetically conservative maternal investment strategy, favouring high fecundity over per-offspring provisioning in the productive waters of the eastern Atlantic.

Growth proceeds steadily during the pelagic larval and juvenile phases. Under the same thermal regime of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], individuals attain sexual maturity after approximately 716.964 days since birth [tp = approximately 716.964 days since birth], a duration that is somewhat prolonged relative to some other sparids of comparable adult size. At puberty, the average total length of Pagellus acarne reaches 16.55 centimeters [Lp = 16.55 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal development and is consistent with size-at-maturity records for the species across its range, and the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 55.156 grams [Wwp = 55.156 grams], reflecting the energetic investment required before reproductive allocation begins. These measurements were derived from a long-term mark-recapture study conducted off the coast of Portugal and align well with published growth curves for the species. The onset of gonadal activity at this size indicates that reproductive investment begins once a substantial body size has been achieved, likely as a strategy to maximise fecundity and survival during the first spawning season. Field records show that maturation timing can vary with local productivity, but the values reported here represent the consensus from multiple sampling years.

Among the oldest individuals in the population, the maximum recorded total length reaches 33.31 centimeters [Li = 33.31 centimeters], while the corresponding asymptotic wet weight attains approximately 391.53 grams [Wwi = approximately 391.53 grams], aligning with typical asymptotic masses reported for congeneric sparids of similar body plan. A female reaching this size may live for up to 3650.0 days [am = up to 3650.0 days] at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], equating to approximately ten years, a moderate lifespan for a teleost of this body plan. Senescence and natural mortality become evident after this point, with very few individuals surviving beyond the maximum recorded longevity. The growth trajectory from juvenile to adult follows a decelerating pattern typical of iteroparous marine fish, with the greatest annual increments occurring during the first few years of life.

Reproductive output in axillary seabream is substantial. At the reference temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], a gravid female can produce approximately 499 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 499 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the high fecundity characteristic of broadcast spawners in the family Sparidae. This value represents the maximum reproductive rate, achieved by the largest and most fecund individuals during peak spawning periods. Fecundity increases with maternal size and age, so that older females contribute disproportionately to total annual egg production. Daily egg release is not constant throughout the spawning season but is concentrated during a series of discrete spawning events. The species exhibits an iteroparous life history, with repeated spawning bouts over multiple years, which buffers against recruitment failure in unfavourable environmental conditions. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirms that oocyte development is asynchronous, allowing for continuous or batch spawning over several weeks.

Comparisons with congeneric species highlight the intermediate life-history strategy of Pagellus acarne. Its maximum lifespan of a decade (10 years) [am = 10 years] is shorter than that of some deeper-water sparids but longer than that of many small-bodied coastal species at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. The total length at puberty, 16.55 centimeters [Lp = 16.55 centimeters], represents approximately half the ultimate total length, a ratio consistent with many iteroparous teleosts that delay reproduction until a substantial portion of somatic growth is complete. This trade-off between growth and reproduction is central to the species' population dynamics. Recruitment success is influenced by both the high daily egg production rate [Ri = daily egg production rate] and the survival of pelagic larvae, the latter being strongly dependent on water temperature and food availability. Continued monitoring of these life-history parameters is essential for informing sustainable fisheries management and for predicting the species' response to climate-driven changes in ocean temperature.
